data.content_ref: inline:The argument fails to resolve the problem's core tension: if one prefers Theory A over Theory B solely because A has survived severe tests in the past, one is effectively acting on the expectation that A will continue to perform better (or be closer to truth) in the future. Popper explicitly rejected the idea that past performance guarantees future results without an inductive principle. By defining the 'rationality' of the choice as maximizing 'error elimination potential,' the target smuggles in the very inductive assumption it claims to avoid—namely, that the mechanism which eliminated errors in the past will remain effective or relevant in the future. Without this hidden premise, the preference is arbitrary; with it, the solution contradicts Popper's rejection of induction.
